The Boeing Company operates in four reportable segments: Commercial Airplanes, Defense, Space & Security, Global Services, and Boeing Capital.
The Commercial Airplanes segment develops, produces, and markets commercial jet aircraft to the commercial airline industry worldwide.
The Commercial Airplanes segment offers a family of commercial jetliners designed to meet global passenger and cargo requirements.
The family of commercial jet aircraft in production includes the 737 narrow-body model and the 767, 777, and 787 wide-body models.
The Boeing Company ended production of the 747 wide-body model in 2022.
Development continues on the 777X program and the 737-7 and 737-10 derivatives.
The Defense, Space & Security segment engages in the research, development, production, and modification of manned and unmanned military aircraft and weapons systems.
The Defense, Space & Security segment includes fighter and trainer aircraft, vertical lift aircraft, and commercial derivative aircraft.

The Defense, Space & Security segment also engages in strategic defense and intelligence systems, C4ISR, cyber and information solutions, intelligence systems, satellite systems, and space exploration.
The Global Services segment provides services to commercial and defense customers worldwide.

The Global Services segment offers supply chain and logistics management, engineering, maintenance, modifications, upgrades, spare parts, pilot and maintenance training, technical and maintenance documents, and data analytics and digital services.
The Boeing Capital segment ensures Boeing customers have financing to buy and take delivery of Boeing products.
The Boeing Capital segment manages overall financing exposure.
The Boeing Capital portfolio consists of equipment under operating leases, sales-type/finance leases, notes and other receivables, assets held for sale or re-lease, and investments.
The Boeing Company owns numerous patents and has licenses for the use of patents owned by others.
The U.S. government has licenses in Boeing patents developed in performance of government contracts.
The U.S. government may use or authorize others to use inventions covered by such patents for government purposes.
Unpatented research, development, and engineering skills, as well as certain trademarks, trade secrets, and other intellectual property rights, contribute to Boeing’s business.

The Boeing Company does not believe its business would be materially affected by the expiration of any particular intellectual property right or termination of any particular intellectual property patent license agreement.
As of December 31, 2022, Boeing’s total workforce was approximately 156,000.
As of December 31, 2021, Boeing’s total workforce was approximately 142,000.
As of December 31, 2022, 13% of Boeing’s workforce was located outside the U.S.
As of December 31, 2022, 12% of Boeing’s workforce was located outside the U.S.
As of December 31, 2022, Boeing’s workforce included approximately 50,000 union members.
The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM) represents 20% of Boeing’s employees.
The IAM has two major agreements, one expiring in September 2024 and one in July 2025.
The Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (SPEEA) represents 10% of Boeing’s employees.
The SPEEA has two major agreements expiring in October 2026.
The United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW) represents 1% of Boeing’s employees.
The UAW has one major agreement expiring in April 2027.
Boeing is committed to creating a company where everyone is included and respected.
Boeing is committed to diverse representation across all levels of its workforce.
In June 2022, Boeing released its second Global Equity, Diversity and Inclusion report.
As of December 2021, Boeing’s U.S. workforce was comprised of approximately 23% women.
As of December 2021, Boeing’s U.S. workforce was comprised of approximately 33% U.S. racial and ethnic minorities.
As of December 2021, Boeing’s U.S. workforce was comprised of approximately 15% U.S. veterans.
Boeing supports Business Resource Groups open to all employees with more than 15,000 participants across 170 chapters globally.
The Business Resource Groups focus on gender, race & ethnicity, generations, gender identity, sexual orientation, disability, or veteran status.
Boeing is committed to releasing an annual Global Equity, Diversity and Inclusion report in 2023.
Boeing’s 2022 Global Equity, Diversity and Inclusion report can be found on its website.

Boeing offers competitive benefits including market-competitive compensation, healthcare, paid time off, parental leave, retirement benefits, tuition assistance, employee skills development, leadership development, and rotation programs.
In 2022, Boeing’s voluntary resignation rate was approximately 4%.
In 2022, Boeing hired approximately 23,000 new employees for critical skills.
In 2022, Boeing had an offer acceptance rate of 78%.
Boeing encourages employees to provide feedback about their experience through ongoing employee engagement activities.
Boeing conducts surveys ranging from pre-hire to exiting the company.
The voluntary surveys provide aggregate trend reports for the company to address in real time.
Boeing has established a multi-level recognition program to acknowledge excellent individual or team performance.
Boeing supports employees’ continuous development of professional, technical, and leadership skills through digital learning resources and partnerships with professional/technical societies.
In 2022, Boeing employees completed approximately 5.8 million hours of learning.
Boeing employees can pursue degree programs, professional certificates, and individual courses from more than 300 accredited colleges and universities through its tuition assistance program.
Over 9,000 Boeing employees leverage these programs every year.
Safety, quality, integrity, and sustainability are at the core of how Boeing operates.
Boeing aspires to achieve zero workplace injuries.
Boeing provides a safe, open, and accountable work environment for employees.
Employees are required to sign the Boeing Code of Conduct annually.
Boeing provides several channels for employees to speak up, ask for guidance, and report concerns related to ethics or safety violations.
Boeing addresses employee concerns and takes appropriate actions that uphold its Boeing values.
The commercial jet aircraft market and airline industry are extremely competitive.
Boeing faces aggressive international competitors such as Airbus and entrants from China.
Boeing is focused on improving products and processes and continuing cost reduction efforts.
Boeing intends to compete by providing customers with airplanes and services that deliver superior design, safety, efficiency, and value.

The Defense, Space & Security segment faces strong competition from Lockheed Martin Corporation, Northrop Grumman Corporation, Raytheon Technologies Corporation, General Dynamics Corporation, and SpaceX.
Non-U.S. companies such as BAE Systems and Airbus Group are building a strategic presence in the U.S. market.
Certain competitors have formed teams with other competitors to address specific customer requirements.
The Defense, Space & Security segment expects strong competition to continue into 2023.
The commercial and defense services markets are extremely challenging and include many strong U.S. and non-U.S. competitors.
The Global Services segment leverages an extensive services network offering products and services spanning the life cycle of defense and commercial aircraft programs.
The Global Services segment provides training, fleet services and logistics, maintenance and engineering, modifications and upgrades, and gate-to-gate operations.
The Global Services segment expects the market to remain highly competitive in 2023.
Boeing intends to grow market share by leveraging high levels of customer satisfaction and productivity.
Boeing’s businesses are heavily regulated in most of its markets.
Boeing works with numerous U.S. government agencies, including all branches of the U.S. military, NASA, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and the Department of Homeland Security.
Similar government authorities exist in non-U.S. markets.
The U.S. government may terminate any of Boeing’s government contracts at its convenience or for default.
If a U.S. government contract is terminated for convenience, Boeing generally receives payment for work completed and allowable termination or cancellation costs.

If a U.S. government contract is terminated for default, the U.S. government pays only for work accepted and may require Boeing to pay the difference between the original contract price and the cost to re-procure the contract items, net of work accepted.
The U.S. government can hold Boeing liable for damages resulting from default.

In the U.S., Boeing’s commercial aircraft products must comply with FAA regulations on production and quality systems, airworthiness, installation approvals, repair procedures, and continuing operational safety.
New aircraft models and derivatives must obtain FAA certification prior to entry into service.
Outside the U.S., similar requirements exist for airworthiness, installation, and operational approvals.
These requirements are generally administered by national aviation authorities and coordinated by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency in Europe.
Boeing is subject to various federal, state, local, and non-U.S. laws and regulations relating to environmental protection.
These laws cover the discharge, treatment, storage, disposal, and remediation of hazardous substances and wastes.
Boeing could be affected by laws and regulations relating to climate change, including those limiting or otherwise related to greenhouse gas emissions.
These laws and regulations could lead to increased environmental compliance expenditures, increased energy and raw materials costs, and new or additional investment in designs and technologies.
Boeing continually assesses its compliance status and management of environmental matters.
Investigation, remediation, and operation and maintenance costs associated with environmental compliance are a normal, recurring part of Boeing’s operations.
These costs are often allowable under U.S. government contracts.
It is reasonably possible that costs incurred to ensure continued environmental compliance could have a material impact on Boeing’s results of operations, financial condition, or cash flows.
For additional information on environmental contingencies, see Note 13 to Boeing’s Consolidated Financial Statements.
Boeing’s non-U.S. sales are subject to both U.S. and non-U.S. governmental regulations and procurement policies and practices.
These include regulations relating to import-export control and tariffs.
